en: Recall Conrad Helfrich From the Indies
In these pressing times, we must prioritize the homeland above all else. Conrad Helfrich, as the Royal Dutch Navy's best Admiral, must return to the Netherlands.
Is currently passing a law in the Volksraad

The People’s Council, known in Dutch as the Volksraad, was established in 1918 as an attempt to bring democracy to the East Indies, as part of the implementation of the so-called “Ethical Policies”. The seats are filled by both Dutch and Indonesian officials, selected through various means. While the Netherlands maintains an unconditional veto right, the Volksraad can pass motions and bills to the government.
Allow the Indonesian Language in Schools

Access to higher education in the indies is largely limited to the Dutch and wealthy classes of Indonesians who speak Dutch, as it is the only language higher education is taught in. An ongoing motion in the Volksraad to open Indonesian-language schools is awaiting a vote from the Governor General.
Allow the Indonesian Language in Government

Governmental roles in the Indies, including the Volksraad all require fluency in the Dutch language, which has led to many members of the Volksraad, especially representatives of native communities, to question the validity of its democracy. They have put together a motion which insists that government positions should be able to be filled by Indonesian speakers when possible.

The education system in the East Indies currently operates using education quotas, where a certain number of Indonesian students must be accepted, and a certain number of Dutch students must be accepted. This has been controversial in the Volksraad due to the common belief that it is skewed unfairly toward the Dutch favor. While we could let the Volksraad continue arguing for years over how to reform the system, it may be worth abolishing the quota system all-together.

There is currently an extremely high tax on private companies exporting rubber, allowing us to maintain a monopoly over the market. However, this has resulted in economic stagnation in some regions due to private plantations being unable to operate. This was deemed worthwhile at the time of implementation, but international protectionism from the Great Depression has left our rubber export economy far less lucrative. It may be worth reducing the tax in order to stimulate the economy.
Pass Anti-Discrimination Laws for Military Ranks

While there is no formal rule stopping Indonesian natives from rising the ranks of the KNIL, there is an unwritten rule forbidding this, limiting even the most well-performing of military personnel unable to progress beyond Colonel status. Several parties in the Volksraad have been pressuring the government to recognize the efforts of high performing Indonesian officers.
Legalize the Display of the Red/White Flag

The red and white flag of “Indonesia” is currently illegal to display in public due to its connections to nationalist, anti-colonial organizations. Legalizing its display would likely be a demonstration of our willingness to cooperate, and stop the ongoing radicalization of nationalists across the archipelago.
Open Education Subsidies for Non-Dutch Residents

There has been an ongoing debate within the Volksraad regarding the subsidies and scholarships given to Dutch students in the East Indies. Several representatives of native communities in the Volksraad have argued that this system should be expanded to any student, regardless of background. This would buy us a lot of good-will with the population, though it would not be cheap.
Make Indonesian an official National Language

The Indonesian language has grown to become a common language in many parts of the archipelago, bridging language gaps between several cultures. With the Indonesian language now being permitted within education and government roles, many Volksraad representatives have been petitioning for its legal recognition as an official language of the colony, sharing equal status with Dutch.
Our flag will be changed to the Red/White flag.

The motions in the Volksraad pushing for autonomy have ultimately succeeded, and what was called the Dutch East Indies only a few years ago is now the Dominion of Indonesia. Our flag should be adjusted to represent these changes.

Volksraad Debating Soetardjo's Petition for Autonomy

Soetardjo is a Volksraad member who is known for leading the peaceful nationalist movement. He is currently organizing a petition requesting that [INS.GetNameDef] be given more autonomy, and for a round table conference to be organized between Dutch and Indonesian representatives, in order to discuss the desire of Indonesians to become autonomous as part of a Dutch commonwealth. This petition is currently being debated within the Volksraad. Once these debates conclude, we must decide how to respond, as the petition's consequences are of great significance.

We will organize riots and skirmishes with the enemy forces in order to raise tension and escalation, laying the groundwork to ensure more severe operations later face less international scrutiny.

The Dutch will not negotiate with us in good faith. To them we remain rebels, an inconvenience to be suppressed rather than a nation to be reckoned with. But the great powers of the world are another matter, and The Hague cannot dismiss them so easily. We will appeal to the international community to mediate, and let foreign pressure compel what our own voice cannot.

Our raids have done their work. The colonial garrison knows our reach, and The Hague knows we are not cowed. Yet each strike gives the Netherlands fresh cause to send more men and more ships, and we are not ready for open war. Word will go to our commanders to hold their fire. The next blow falls when we say so, not when the Dutch goad us into it.

After 350 years of Dutch tyranny, we have taken matters into our own hands and declared independence. The Netherlands does not recognize our authority, still continuing to govern the Indies as their colony while treating us as criminals.\n\nWe must continue to take control over more regions and important cities and topple the Dutch government from within. However, we should be careful to not be too aggressive without careful planning, as rapid escalation from us might provoke Dutch military action.

Revolutionaries in the East Indies have illegally declared independence, and have taken control over regions of the Indies with militia forces. Despite our best efforts, we have been unable to reestablish control in these regions due to the sheer number of militia forces present.\n\nWe need to stop them before they take control over more cities and destabilize the Indies administration further. While extreme, military force may be necessary if they continue to act like this.
§RWithout Batavia we cannot govern the Indies, and we will have no choice but to negotiate a peace agreement with the revolutionaries.§!

Dutch reprisals have grown heavier after each of our raids, and their patrols press into districts they had abandoned months ago. Our commanders report harder fighting in places long thought settled, and our casualties mount faster than the recruiters can replace them. The conflict has spread into provinces that were quiet last year.

The reports from our residencies worsen by the week. The rebels strike in districts where they were not thought to operate, and the military command in Batavia presses for measures heavier than any tried before. In The Hague, those who once counselled patience grow fewer at every cabinet meeting.

The Dutch greed that caused them to invest almost exclusively in Java, ignoring the eastern islands has left Java as the Achilles' heel of the entire colony. This will be their downfall! We must storm our forces into Java and destroy Dutch communications and supply networks, making the Indies administration unable to operate.

The Republican forces have begun an operation to relocate most of their forces into Java, attempting to take control over the entire island. We must continue to resist, their operation is risky, and has given us an opportunity to topple their government if they fail.
Moestopo demands promotion for his efforts

Our revolution did not end when the last colonial soldier was driven from [ROOT.GetAdjective] soil. The workers and peasants of [FROM.GetName] suffer under the same yoke we have cast off, and they look to us now as proof that the oppressor can be beaten. We shall send our agitators among them, distribute pamphlets, fund their unions, and fan the flames of discontent until the conditions for revolution are ripe.

The conditions in [FROM.GetName] are ripe. Our agents report growing unrest in the factories and fields, and the local party cells are prepared to act. The time has come to call the workers and peasants of [FROM.GetName] to rise and seize what is rightfully theirs.

The people of [FROM.GetName] toil for the benefit of a foreign master, made to serve interests not their own. We shall remind them that submission is a choice, and that their masters are not as strong as they pretend to be.

There are those within [FROM.GetName] who have already taken up the cause on their own. They lack organization and resources, but not conviction. By coordinating with these groups we can hasten the collapse of the existing order, even if the resulting instability makes the country harder to govern in the short term.

Pamphlets and speeches will carry the revolution only so far. When the moment comes, our comrades in [FROM.GetName] must be able to fight. Surplus arms and supplies are to be smuggled to sympathetic militias so that the forces of reaction will face an armed populace, not a defenceless one.
If a civil war starts, the Communists will start with additional divisions.

Party organisers are to be dispatched throughout [FROM.GetName] to establish reading circles, recruit among the trade unions, and bring the message of revolution to the villages. The seeds we plant today will bear fruit soon enough.

Our resources are not limitless, and the struggle in [FROM.GetNameDef] demands more than we can presently afford to give. We shall withdraw our agents and redirect our efforts where they are needed most.
